pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Store separately verified anonymized copies under data_5conf/anonymized/pdf; preserve every original file.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes latent-likelihood scoring, feature-space benefits and a strong MVTecAD speed-AUC trade-off. v2 broadens the principal claims to plug-and-play applicability across diffusion AD models and state-of-the-art unified multi-class performance with approximately twofold acceleration without distillation. The reconstruction-free contribution remains, but its claimed applicability and comparative scope expand substantially.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning feature quality versus diffusion architecture and why noise-residual prediction may favor integration with MDM over DeCoDiff. It extends applicability arguments to medical imaging. Conversely, v1's explicit caveats about Jacobian omission, theoretical interpretation and broader OOD applicability disappear; future work shifts toward single-step distillation.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B add dataset statistics, resizing and normalization instructions, architecture dimensions, detailed optimization and noise-schedule settings, software versions, hardware and throughput measurement conditions. v2 also supplies project and code links. These substantially extend v1's sparse implementation information, although its best-performing-checkpoint selection statement is no longer provided.

E1.justification: MVTecAD and VisA remain, while v2 adds MPDD and BMAD's six medical evaluation datasets, including brain MRI, liver CT and retinal OCT. It also adds unified multi-class evaluation alongside per-category comparisons, substantially extending the represented domains and evaluation scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 adds comparisons with RD4AD, UniAD, SimpleNet, DeSTSeg, HVQ-Trans and OmiAD in Table 2, plus medical comparators in Table 12. In the corresponding per-category MVTecAD comparison, DeCoDiff is added and DiAD is removed; DiAD remains in the new multi-class comparison. These changes substantially expand comparator coverage.

E3.justification: Training changes from 1000 to 300 epochs. The principal benchmark configuration changes from S=2 and category-tuned S in {2,3,4,5} to fixed S=3. v2 also introduces AP, maximum F1, AU-PRO and aggregate mAD evaluation beyond the earlier AUROC reporting. These are substantive revisions and additions to the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 adds feature-encoder and diffusion-architecture ablations and tests integration into DeCoDiff and MDM (Tables 5-7). Appendix F separately evaluates NLL, spatial range and their combination. Reconstruction-versus-inversion sensitivity testing remains with revised results, while v1's hazelnut score histograms are removed. Comparative localization case studies are also added.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly states that library random seeds were fixed and nondeterministic GPU operations disabled where possible. It supplies neither seed values nor repeated-run counts. Neither version reports confidence intervals or significance tests, so this is a limited reporting addition.

E6.justification: v1's tuned Ours* image/pixel AUROC averages are 99.1/94.8 on MVTecAD and 95.8/98.4 on VisA. v2's single-class tables report 99.1/97.3 and 97.0/99.0 under revised models and settings. These are replacement results, not controlled performance gains. New multi-class, medical, integration and ablation results substantially expand the reported findings.

M1.justification: The default diffusion architecture changes from UNet to class-unconditional DiT, described in v2's Implementations section and Appendix B. Algorithm 1 also changes the stated score aggregation from separately normalized terms to spatial range plus map sum. The underlying DDIM inversion, feature-space modeling and spatial-norm ideas are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and methodological narrative are extensively rewritten. v2 removes duplicated paragraphs from v1 Sections 3.4 and 4.3, consolidates related-work/background material, and reorganizes technical discussion into appendices. It also shortens the title, changes the author block and introduces the InvAD name.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-metric benchmark tables, integration and architecture tables, implementation tables and extensive localization heatmaps. The original conceptual Figure 1 is retained but relocated and recaptioned. The score histograms disappear, the VisA comparison moves to the appendix with revised columns, and the properties table receives a substantially revised structure.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the broad memory/reconstruction/density survey with a diffusion-focused taxonomy covering conditioning, discriminators and adaptive timesteps. It adds substantive positioning against OmiAD and DeCoDiff and credits diffusion-based OOD work as inspiration. Several flow-related references and the earlier flow-connection argument disappear, changing the research framing beyond citation formatting.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds explicit DDIM posterior and noise-parameterization equations and a stepwise Euler inversion derivation. The central PF-ODE and inversion equations remain equivalent. v1's likelihood-Jacobian relationship and associated justification are removed, and the noise schedule is corrected from monotonically increasing to decreasing. No new theoretical guarantee is established.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's limited validation and reproducibility: architecture ablations and integration tests directly examine previously untested dependence and portability, medical evaluation broadens applicability evidence, and Appendix B supplies much fuller implementation specifications. These gains outweigh remaining scoring-description inconsistencies and numerical reporting errors, including incorrect DeCoDiff deltas in Table 5. Changed architectures and protocols mean that cross-version scores themselves do not establish controlled performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion-based latent-inversion anomaly-detection work. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable. v1 ends with references; v2 additionally contains supplementary sections A-G, which were included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original industrial and medical anomaly-detection results, architecture ablations, scoring experiments and integration tests, including results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original MVTecAD and VisA results, inference timings, and inversion/scoring analyses in Tables 2-4 and Figure 2.

results.title: InvAD: Inversion-based Reconstruction-Free Anomaly Detection with Diffusion Models

C1.justification: The central dataset, benchmark, and multi-frame spatial-learning contributions remain intact. v2's introduction additionally claims comparability with specialized 3D perception models, scalability with trainable parameters, and preservation of general abilities. It also adds a first-time novelty claim for observing spatial emergence, extending the existing contribution framing.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning the importance of vision-encoder tuning, the proposed orthogonality of spatial and general capabilities, and depth/correspondence as more fundamental spatial tasks. SpatialRGPT's results motivate a new claim about failure of single-image supervision to transfer. The limitations now acknowledge extra-frame generalization evidence while retaining the need for training beyond pairs.

D1.justification: Table 7 newly discloses task-wise corpus counts, while Appendices H–L document configurations and sample counts for added experiments. Existing code listings, core hyperparameters, and hardware details remain. v2 removes v1's project-page link and Appendix B's pointer to complete templates; the PDFs do not establish whether actual resource availability changed.

E1.justification: v2 expands held-out evaluation to synthetic indoor views rendered from 3RScan, spatial and embodied reasoning in CVBench-3D and ERQA, and broader general VQA coverage through MMMU, MME, and MMVet. Appendix L also tests camera-direction prediction with additional intermediate images, extending evaluation beyond image pairs.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 remove InternVL-13B and add SpatialRGPT to the MultiSPA and BLINK comparisons; 13B remains in other experiments. Appendix I additionally evaluates VGGT for camera-vector prediction, Depth Anything for depth comparison, and LoFTR for image matching, substantially broadening the comparator set.

E3.justification: The default training setup and MultiSPA scoring rules are retained. New protocols vary trainable components and full versus LoRA tuning, normalize scale for the VGGT comparison, test 1K correspondence examples with 50K auxiliary-task examples, compare 400K-example auxiliary-task additions, and insert 1–4 intermediate frames. These are additional experimental settings, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scaling, pooled multi-task, and Easy/Hard correspondence studies, v2 adds component-tuning ablations (Table 8), task-specific transfer analyses (Tables 12–13), a forgetting curve throughout training (Figure 6), and robustness to additional input frames (Table 14). These investigate previously untested sources of gains and failure concerns.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The statement about using different random seeds to sample image pairs is retained and does not constitute new experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The retained model's MultiSPA and BLINK averages remain 56.11 and 84.3. v2 adds extensive results, including a 66.72 fully tuned average in Table 8, 18.7/27.7 accuracy for 8B/26B on 3RScan, and scale-normalized VGGT-versus-ours scores of 86 versus 82 in Table 9. Figure 4 adds a full-tuning result near 72%; v1's reported 44% used a different tuning configuration, so this is not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The data-generation algorithms, architecture, objectives, and default InternVL2-8B LoRA procedure remain unchanged. The original appendix algorithms and Listings 1–4 are retained. Newly evaluated component-unfreezing and full-fine-tuning configurations are experimental variants rather than new proposed algorithmic components.

P1.justification: There are localized rewrites of the abstract, introduction, related work, and scaling discussion, plus author/header edits. The appendix gains sections H–L and moves the limitations from H to M. Most existing prose, the main section sequence, algorithms, and dataset examples are retained.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the opening page, placing Figure 1 above a two-column abstract/introduction arrangement. Figure 4 is redrawn with a logarithmic data axis and explicit LoRA/full-tuning curves. Tables 7–14 and the forgetting plot are added, and existing tables are repositioned. The original appendix example figures are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including VLM-3R, Spatial-MLLM, OST-Bench, and the newly evaluated expert models and benchmarks. Flamingo, ShareGPT4V, and ShareGPT4o references disappear with shortened training-background discussion. Positioning expands toward specialist-model comparability and emergence novelty, while the principal distinction from single-image spatial methods and SAT remains.

T1.justification: The projection, visibility, overlap, and rotation definitions in Equations 1–8 retain their mathematical content. Section 3.3's explicit inequality restates the existing 20% relative L2-error criterion. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The expert comparisons, additional domain and benchmark evaluations, component/task ablations, and extra-frame tests substantially strengthen evidence for the central claims and address important gaps in v1's validation. Appendices H–L also clarify what drives performance. Removed resource pointers and some overbroad interpretations are drawbacks: for example, the introduction claims no degradation despite Table 11 showing MMVet falling from 62.0 to 58.1. These issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Multi-SpatialMLLM and MultiSPA. The complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison; retained material can be matched across reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds expert-model comparisons, additional benchmark evaluations, and training and robustness analyses in Appendices H–L.

before.justification: v1 reports original MultiSPA, BLINK, and general VQA evaluations, scaling and multi-task experiments, and robotics demonstrations in Section 4.

results.title: Multi-SpatialMLLM: Multi-Frame Spatial Understanding with Multi-Modal Large Language Models

C1.justification: v1 claims superiority over published zero-shot checkpoints and, in its conclusion, training on any previous synthetic dataset. v2 acknowledges the stronger FoundationStereo checkpoint and instead claims competitiveness with its training dataset while retaining superiority over the conventional mixed-data baseline. The abstract and introduction reposition the contribution around dataset-design analysis, a resulting dataset and open generation code.

C2.justification: The object-type discussion shifts from suggesting that mesh diversity matters less to explaining performance through benchmark-specific object biases. New discussion interprets solver realism as potentially helping in-domain performance while hindering transfer, and associates render-noise benefits with KITTI's noisier captures. These refine the interpretation while retaining the central realism-and-diversity explanation.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies ceiling-removal and lighting-alteration probabilities of 0.3 and 0.2, explicitly documents ETH3D's 1px threshold, and clarifies configurable window removal. It omits v1's NVIDIA L40 identification and explicit 1m camera-clearance detail. Unoptimized generation estimates change from 1902 CPU/960 GPU days to 275 CPU/900 GPU days. Most appendix implementation details and the code link are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds the FoundationStereo training corpus and DrivingStereo evaluation data within the existing synthetic-to-real stereo task and indoor/outdoor/driving coverage. The additional Middlebury split and revised generated-dataset counts concern experimental settings rather than new task coverage.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 3, v2 Table 2 adds StereoAnywhere and FoundationStereo checkpoints, removes Selective-RAFT, and adds RAFT-Mixed and paired Selective-IGEV training comparisons. FoundationStereo data also becomes a comparator in the dataset, sample-efficiency and appendix qualitative experiments. These substantially strengthen and restructure the comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 adds generation-compute matching using 30k versus 5k pairs, held-out evaluation excluding ten Middlebury validation scenes and sampling 200 DrivingStereo pairs, and EPE evaluation throughout the parameter study. Section 4 revises the dataset size from 152,890 to 163,666 pairs and adds Selective-IGEV training. Section 4.3 describes the sample-efficiency model as DLNR instead of RAFT-Stereo; this reported setting revision does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a bush-only object ablation, full-versus-reduced solver evaluation, and compute-matched rendering/solver experiments testing the quality-versus-quantity tradeoff. Held-out benchmarks address generalization beyond parameter-tuning benchmarks, while Appendix A/Table 7 checks conclusions using EPE. The earlier ray-tracing ablation is largely relocated into Table 4, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, uncertainty bars or significance tests for the empirical comparisons. The additional EPE measurements in v2 are performance metrics, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Many retained benchmark scores are unchanged, but substantial results are added. In v2 Table 2, FoundationStereo reports 1.10 Middlebury-2014-H error versus the retained DLNR-WMGStereo result of 3.76. New Table 6 reports held-out Middlebury errors of 12.61 for DLNR-WMGStereo and 14.23 for DLNR-FSD. Bush, compute-matched, EPE and FSD scaling results are added; the earlier Booster ray-tracing-ablation scores are omitted. Reported unoptimized generation-cost estimates also change.

M1.justification: The generation procedure is retained. Floating-object placement, problematic-object/material removal, window-glass geometry removal, the greedy room solver, denoising and scene mixing already appear in v1. The WMGStereo renaming, added implementation explanations and evaluation of another stereo architecture do not establish a new proposed method.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten, including an explicit three-contribution summary and consistent WMGStereo terminology. Cost-optimization subsections are reordered, and atmospheric-effects and post-processing passages move from the main text into Appendix B. This exceeds routine copyediting.

P2.justification: The original generation-cost bar chart is removed, and ray-tracing rows move into an expanded cost-study table. Model comparisons are regrouped by architecture; held-out and appendix EPE tables are added. The scaling plot gains an FSD curve and a wider axis, and the appendix qualitative comparison gains FSD panels. Existing figures are also relocated and restyled.

R1.justification: v2 adds substantive positioning against FoundationStereo, emphasizing comparable training data alongside accessible generation code and parameter analysis. It also adds StereoAnywhere, SMD-Nets/UnrealStereo4k and DepthAnythingV2 citations. The dedicated real-world-dataset and deep-stereo-network discussions are removed, along with several associated references, substantially refocusing related work.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results or proofs, and no substantive mathematical assumptions or derivations are added. The expanded use of standard stereo-error metrics is an empirical evaluation change.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: Table 6 tests benchmarks excluded from parameter tuning, Table 4 evaluates the generation-cost tradeoff under matched compute, and Tables 2 and 5 introduce stronger comparators and additional controlled training comparisons. The revised claims appropriately acknowledge FoundationStereo's stronger checkpoint instead of retaining broad superiority claims. Although some implementation details and Booster ablation entries are lost, the improved controls, generalization evidence and claim calibration provide a clear substantial net gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same procedural stereo-dataset study despite changes to the title and dataset name. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including their appendices, were readable and supported comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds comparisons, compute-matched experiments, held-out benchmark evaluations and appendix EPE results.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset-generation ablations, stereo benchmark evaluations, generation-time measurements, sample-efficiency experiments and qualitative predictions.

results.title: What Makes Good Synthetic Training Data for Zero-Shot Stereo Matching?

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion expand the work from benchmark construction and evaluation to include a reinforcement fine-tuning baseline. v3 additionally claims cross-city generalization improvements and improved reasoning efficiency after training. The central transit-map benchmark and open-/closed-source performance-pattern claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 offers broader knowledge and visual integration as possible explanations for closed-source advantages. v3 emphasizes visual grounding and successful self-correction, contrasting these with open-source models overturning correct intermediate judgments. It also introduces interpretations concerning language bias, OCR insufficiency, and grounding versus spatial-reasoning failures. Existing generalization limitations remain, with expanded cross-view, agent-based, and embodied future directions.

D1.justification: v3 documents three-expert quality review, an approximately 16% initial annotation error rate, additional difficulty labels, name-normalization rules, local/English answer matching, and training hyperparameters. It also specifies a planned Apache 2.0 dataset release. These disclosures do not establish changes to retained experiments. Conversely, v1's eight-A100 inference-hardware specification is removed.

E1.justification: The 30-city, 1,008-pair dataset is retained, but Appendix C.3–C.4 adds substantially different input scenarios: complete network topology supplied as text, and English station aliases for Beijing and Hangzhou. These extend v1's visual-input and question-only settings. OCRBench contributes previously published scores for analysis, rather than a newly conducted evaluation.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct while retaining all 15 original models; Table 3 retains its six-model comparison. The new training comparison uses untuned 3B and 7B counterparts, and symbolic-map experiments reuse existing model families. Comparator coverage expands within the established model set.

E3.justification: v3 introduces cross-city fine-tuning with disjoint training and test maps, AdamW, learning rate 1e-6, KL coefficient 1e-3, eight sampled responses per query, and batch size 16. New analyses specify topology textualization, structure-preserving station-name substitutions, and alternative scoring schemes. The existing 312-sample test set, 2,048-token limit, and difficulty weights are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds component-level error scores, map-score sensitivity tests, language substitutions, symbolic-input comparisons, and analyses distinguishing OCR, grounding, and spatial-reasoning failures (Appendix C). These substantially extend v1's masking, difficulty, city, and qualitative analyses. The original difficulty and city plots are retained as Figures A1–A2, not new experiments.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its benchmark results. The eight responses sampled during GRPO training are an optimization setting, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: All shared numerical entries in Tables 2 and 3 remain unchanged. v3 adds the 7B results, training outcomes, and Tables A3–A7. For example, Table 4 reports 7B short/long accuracy increasing from 13.28%/7.12% to 26.22%/26.04% after fine-tuning. Table A5 shows English-alias improvements for every long-question comparison but declines in four of six short-question comparisons. Symbolic-input results use different conditions from visual evaluation.

M1.justification: v3 adds a task-specific GRPO training baseline for Qwen2.5-VL-3B and 7B, using binary route-correctness and output-format rewards (Section 4.3 and Appendix B.4). v1 only constructs and evaluates the benchmark. The existing construction pipeline and correctness/map-score algorithms remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, the introductory benchmark-gap argument and performance interpretation are substantially rewritten, and the results discussion is reordered. The appendix is reorganized: preprocessing moves into evaluation details, supplementary experiments receive their own section, and case analyses and further statements are separated. Map Metadata is renamed Metro Data.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, substantially redraws the overview, construction pipeline, and case figures, and adds Table 4 and Tables A3–A7. v1 Figures 3–4 move to appendix Figures A1–A2. Redrawn case figures add endpoint annotations and error labels; Figure A3 also changes two retained Doubao response labels without explanation.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands the cited literature and sharpens positioning around jointly testing fine-grained perception and spatial reasoning. It explicitly contrasts ReasonMap with MapBench and V*Bench, adds geospatial benchmarks such as Geo-Bench, GeoReasoner, and GeoChain, and connects future work to localization, agentic vision, and embodied research. Earlier cited works are retained, including those with updated publication metadata.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds a formal centered group-advantage definition and reward-weighted log-likelihood objective, Equations 1–2, for the new training baseline. v1 contains no corresponding training mathematics. The original scoring algorithms are retained, and no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's diagnostic value: symbolic-input and language controls test explanations that v1 largely discussed, scoring ablations examine metric sensitivity, and cross-city fine-tuning demonstrates use of the previously unused training partition. Added evaluation and annotation details also improve transparency. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including an overgeneralized English-language advantage despite mixed short-question results and inconsistent Doubao labels in Figure A3. The improvement rests on stronger validation and practical usefulness, rather than higher scores alone.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ReasonMap benchmark despite the changed title. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding datasets, algorithms, tables, and relocated figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds fine-tuning experiments, symbolic-map evaluation, language substitutions, and scoring analyses. Table A7 separately identifies its OCRBench scores as collected from other works.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 15 MLLMs, visual-input masking experiments, difficulty and city analyses, and qualitative error cases.

results.title: ReasonMap: Towards Fine-Grained Visual Reasoning from Transit Maps

C1.justification: The central claim that dense initialization removes the need for densification while accelerating reconstruction remains. v2 specifies LPIPS and SSIM when claiming faster matching of standard 3DGS, drops the prominent half-splat claim, and explicitly promotes integration with adaptive density control without increasing training time or Gaussian count.

C2.justification: v1 attributes weaker PSNR improvements to difficulty with reflective surfaces; v2 replaces that discussion with an explanation of how SH initialization improves view-dependent appearance, especially indoors. It also adds substantive interpretations separating geometric consistency, spatial coverage, and raw point count, plus arguments about initialization sufficiency under sparse supervision.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands the implementation recipe: confidence and reprojection thresholds, NDC units, handling of underdetermined SH estimation, coefficient-unfreezing instructions, and ADC settings. Appendix A also supplies an approximately 120-second initialization breakdown, including matching, triangulation, and SH estimation, plus CPU preprocessing details. These materially extend v1's reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The three core datasets remain, but v2 adds systematic sparse-view reconstruction on seven Mip-NeRF360 scenes with only 12 or 24 training views (Appendix B). v1 had only a brief sparse, front-facing demo report. v2 also reports Synthetic-dataset evaluations in Appendix F, although their referenced videos are not embedded in the PDF.

E2.justification: v2 adds VGGT-X to the initialization comparison and evaluates RegNeRF, SparseNeRF, and SparseGS in the new sparse-view comparison; the first two were only cited in v1. Conversely, v1's quantitative efficiency comparisons against methods including gsplat, EAGLES, MiniSplatting, and 3DGS-LM on Tanks&Temples and Deep Blending are absent from v2.

E3.justification: Default initialization changes from 15K correspondences and one nearest neighbor to 20K and two neighbors. v2 adds 10K-step early stopping, explicit 12/24-view training protocols, and ADC integration using 140 reference views and 8.5K correspondences per view. Scaffold-GS resource reporting changes from anchors to generated splats. The standard test split and image downsampling are retained and moved to Appendix A.

E4.justification: v2 adds sampling-component and SH ablations (Table 6), a 3DGS-without-densification control (Table 4), denser COLMAP controls (Table A2), and quantitative nearest-neighbor sensitivity. v1's Gaussian-count trajectories and undercoverage case visualization (Figs. A5–A6) are removed. Motion, noise robustness, and extreme-viewpoint analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 Fig. A5 shows shaded bands around Gaussian-count trajectories described as averages across scenes; v2 removes this plot. Neither PDF defines what those bands represent, so their status as statistical uncertainty reporting is unclear. Neither version otherwise specifies repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: For 30K EDGS+3DGS, Mip-NeRF360 PSNR/LPIPS change from 27.80/0.175 to 28.02/0.141, while LPIPS changes from 0.124 to 0.132 on Tanks&Temples and 0.219 to 0.223 on Deep Blending. These are revised-method results, not strictly matched-setting gains. v2 also revises RAIN-GS's Mip-NeRF360 PSNR from 22.23 to 27.23 and adds substantial sparse-view, component, and integration results.

M1.justification: v2 introduces degree-3 spherical-harmonics initialization from multi-view observations using a pseudoinverse (Sec. 3.5). Compared with v1's pair-averaged initial colors, v2 uses reference-view color plus fitted higher-order coefficients, materially changing appearance initialization. Triangulation and confidence-thresholded correspondence sampling were already present in v1.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites and condenses the introduction and related work, including removing the artist/sculptor analogy. It reorganizes the method into five subsections, restructures the experimental narrative around quality, efficiency, and compatibility, reorders ablations, and extensively reorganizes the appendices.

P2.justification: The large combined comparison table is separated into quality and efficiency tables, with additional integration and component tables. v2 redraws the teaser and sensitivity plots, adds a motion schematic, moves v1 Fig. 2 to Fig. A3 and Fig. A7 to Fig. 5, removes Playroom qualitative panels and some diagnostic figures, and changes the appendix to a two-column layout.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to VGGT-X, VGGT, SparseGS, and Penrose's generalized inverse. It extends comparisons with learned geometry priors and sparse-view methods and emphasizes complementarity with adaptive densification. The broader positioning relative to NeRF, Gaussian splatting, acceleration, and initialization research remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for reprojection filtering, combined sampling distributions, and the SH least-squares/pseudoinverse formulation (Eqs. 8–13). The existing triangulation and Gaussian-motion mathematics remain essentially unchanged. No new theorem or convergence proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves support for the method's mechanism and its reproducibility. Table 6 and Appendix E provide controls separating appearance initialization, sampling cues, and point-count effects, while Appendix A supplies important implementation details missing from v1. The systematic sparse-view evaluation also strengthens evidence beyond the earlier demo report. Some cross-dataset efficiency comparisons and diagnostic visualizations are lost, but the targeted controls and substantially clearer initialization recipe provide a clear overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EDGS research work. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, references, and supplementary appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 reports original reconstruction results, component ablations, integration experiments, and appendix experiments on sparse-view reconstruction and denser COLMAP initialization.

before.justification: v1 reports original EDGS reconstruction experiments, quantitative benchmark results in Table 1, initialization and matching ablations, robustness analyses, and appendix per-scene results.

results.title: EDGS: Eliminating Densification for Efficient Convergence of 3DGS

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion add SVDS as a contribution addressing incomplete removal and color inconsistency. The central claims about attention-guided object-effect removal, background preservation, and OBER remain. The quantitative superiority claim is qualified from all test sets and metrics to nearly all.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of the denoising-strength tradeoff, interprets the blending control as evidence beyond background preservation, and discusses applicability to effect-free objects. Reflection generalization is narrowed to transfer from limited indoor reflection training to outdoor reflections. The limitations discussion replaces the explicit large/long-shadow warning with explanations and examples of under-removing target effects or over-removing neighboring effects.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset and interactive-demo links, SVDS parameter details, and model-size and runtime information with resolution and hardware context. Most training and augmentation details are retained. Conversely, it omits v1's explicit baseline prompt, 'an empty scene,' and the precise SDXL-Inpainting checkpoint URL.

E1.justification: Section 8.2 adds evaluations on OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and an effect-free subset of MULAN; MULAN previously appeared only in discussion and dataset comparisons. Figure 13 additionally demonstrates simultaneous removal of multiple targets. Object insertion, movement, and coarse-stroke scenarios were already present in v1.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds OmniEraser, GeoRemover, and OmniPaint while retaining the earlier numerical comparators. The user study adds OmniEraser and OmniPaint, and several qualitative panels replace older comparators with these methods. Table 7 introduces baseline variants equipped with ground-truth-mask background blending.

E3.justification: The reported guidance scale changes from 7.5 to 1.0, OBER-Test from 160 to 163 samples, and OBER-Wild from 300 to 302. ReMOVE becomes ReMOVE†, comparing the removal region against the input rather than output background. New protocols include 500 effect-free MULAN pairs, resolution normalization, and ground-truth blending controls. User-study presentations increase from 40 to 80 per participant, retaining 30 participants. The reflection-bootstrap training description also changes from no reflection data to limited indoor reflections; these disclosures do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 2 and Figure 11 add comparisons of uniform denoising strengths against SVDS. Section 8.3 tests whether background blending explains the performance advantage, while Figures 13 and 17 add simultaneous-removal cases and explicit failure examples. The earlier mask-loss, simulated-data, fusion, and coarse-stroke analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for the performance results. Expanded user-study sampling changes the evaluation protocol without adding uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces ObjectClear's RORD-Val PSNR of 26.40 with 26.24 and OBER-Test PSNR of 32.98 with 33.04 under revised settings; these are not controlled version-to-version gains or losses. ReMOVE scores are replaced by ReMOVE† scores, with OmniPaint now ahead of ObjectClear on OBER-Wild, 0.8656 versus 0.8470. Tables 5–7 add benchmark and blending-control results. New user-study preferences for ObjectClear are 78.90% against OmniEraser and 70.33% against OmniPaint, while earlier preferences are retained. Runtime results are also newly reported.

M1.justification: v2 adds Spatially-Varying Denoising Strength (SVDS), using strength 1.0 inside the object mask and 0.99 outside, with background reinjection during inference. This is a localized inference extension to the retained architecture, embedding construction, mask loss, and attention-guided fusion. Renaming Object-Effect Attention to Adaptive Target-Aware Attention does not itself change the method.

Training also includes ScanQA/SQA3D splits for their evaluations and an experiment incorporating general LLaVA-Video data. The original temporal benchmark remains based on static scenes.

E2.justification: V3 Table 1 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Spatial-MLLM-4B, VG-LLM-4B, and a fine-tuned LLaVA-OneVision comparison. Gemini-2.5 Pro replaces Gemini-1.5 entries in Tables 1–2, while several smaller-model comparisons and VSI tiny-set/human rows are removed. New experiments introduce substantial additional comparator groups, including Video-3D LLM and GPT-4V.

E3.justification: New protocols include combined ScanQA/SQA3D training, evaluation on 4,675 validation and 3,519 test questions with language-generation and EM/EM-R metrics, zero-shot OpenEQA evaluation, and a controlled addition of 30k general videos. These expand the evaluation design; the original one-epoch recipe and VSTI train/test counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 adds 2D–2D and explicit-point fusion ablations, a CUT3R-versus-VGGT comparison, general-data mixing, and spatial/non-spatial transfer analysis on OpenEQA. These test architectural choices and capability tradeoffs absent from v1. Token-removal ablations remain, but most of their task-specific scores are omitted from the condensed Table 6.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. The added experiments retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The headline VLM-3R averages remain 60.9 on VSI-Bench and 58.8 on VSTI-Bench. V3 adds extensive results, including ScanQA CIDEr 101.9, SQA3D EM 60.7, OST-Bench 42.9, and Video-MME 59.9 versus 62.1 with data mixing. Some old comparison and ablation entries disappear. V3 also introduces a prose/table inconsistency: 50.09 versus Table 6's retained 59.09 for removing view tokens.

M1.justification: The proposed model retains CUT3R spatial and camera tokens, cross-attention fusion with visual tokens, a two-layer projector, frozen encoders, and LoRA fine-tuning. The residual connection explicitly formulated in v3 Section 4.1 was already documented in v1 Appendix A.1. Alternative fusion and encoder configurations are evaluated as ablations.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, dataset explanations, and architecture narrative are extensively rewritten and condensed. Contributions are reorganized, experiments gain a broader benchmark structure, and Appendix C becomes three named analyses. Much of Appendices A–B remains substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: V3 changes the document to two columns, redraws Figure 3, adds numerous comparison tables, and replaces the detailed component-ablation table with an average-only summary. Figure 2 loses its donut chart although its caption still refers to rings. The existing trajectory illustration and dataset-distribution tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V3 substantially updates positioning around Spatial-MLLM, VG-LLM, SpatialStack, and newer dynamic-scene work such as VLM4D and DynamicVerse. It develops a specific distinction between CUT3R's metric-scale representations and VGGT-based approaches, extending v1's emphasis on avoiding depth sensors and prebuilt maps.

T1.justification: The recurrent tokenization, cross-attention, residual fusion, and MRA definitions are unchanged in substance. V3's explicit residual equation restates v1 Appendix A.1. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the new encoder discussion is qualitative interpretation.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for transfer, general-purpose capability retention, and the choice of fusion and geometry encoder through Tables 3–7 and D–F. Reporting non-spatial losses alongside spatial gains makes the applicability assessment more informative. These gains outweigh the loss of detailed token-ablation scores and localized reporting errors, including the view-token score inconsistency and overstated OST caption. The improvement comes from stronger validation and clearer tradeoffs, not higher retained headline scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VLM-3R and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–C. The retained architecture, datasets, and results can be matched despite substantial rewriting and layout changes.

after.justification: V3 retains these original results and adds evaluations on additional benchmarks, fusion and geometry-encoder ablations, and a data-mixing experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original VLM-3R evaluations on VSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, together with component ablations in Tables 1–3.
